# Sequence Labeling and Information Extraction {#sec-sequence-labeling}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number on this page was measured on
WikiANN Turkish (PAN-X.tr) — the corpus built by @pan2017cross and the balanced
20,000/10,000/10,000 split defined by @rahimi2019massively, which is what
`load_dataset` returns and the split the leakage in
@sec-sequence-labeling-audit lives in. Used exactly as it ships, so that anyone
can reproduce these numbers in one call.
@sec-sequence-labeling-audit reports what auditing that corpus turned up,
including a leakage problem that changes how the rest of the chapter reads its
own scores. Software: `scikit-learn` 1.9.0, `sklearn-crfsuite` 0.5.0,
`transformers` 5.15.1, PyTorch 2.13.0, `datasets` 5.0.1, `seqeval` 1.2.2 on
Python 3.14.5. Encoder fine-tuning: batch size 16, learning rate 3e-5, three
epochs, seed 42, on an Apple M-series GPU through the MPS backend — one run per
budget, no hyper-parameter search. Local LLM: a 4-bit quantised `qwen3.5:9b`
served by `ollama` 0.24.0 at temperature 0 with thinking disabled. Treat the
timing ratios below as portable and the absolute seconds as not.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- frame NER, POS tagging and chunking as one architecture — a label per token
  — plus a decoding step, and say why the decoding step is where the bugs
  live;
- choose a tagging scheme, decode spans from token predictions, and handle
  the sequences a tagger should never emit but does;
- explain why token accuracy flatters a sequence labeller, and report the
  metric that does not;
- align labels onto subword tokens without silently sliding them off the
  words they belong to;
- extract structured records with an LLM under a schema, align the result
  back onto the text, and measure whether it worked;
- audit a labelled corpus before trusting a score computed on it;
- say what a couple of hundred labelled sentences actually buys, from
  measurement rather than from hope.

## One architecture, three tasks {#sec-sequence-labeling-setup}

@sec-classification asked one question per document: *which class is this?*
This chapter asks one question per *token*, and the questions are no longer
independent — the answer for token 4 constrains the answer for token 5.

That single change of granularity covers most of what the field calls
information extraction:

| task | the question at each token | typical labels |
|:--|:--|:--|
| POS tagging | what part of speech is this word? | `NOUN`, `VERB`, `ADJ`, … |
| Chunking | is this word inside a noun phrase? | `B-NP`, `I-NP`, `O` |
| [NER](#gloss-named-entity-recognition-ner){#term-named-entity-recognition-ner .term-ref} | is this word part of a name, and what kind? | `B-PER`, `I-ORG`, `O`, … |

: Three tasks, one shape {tbl-colwidths="[20,44,36]"}

::: {#gloss-named-entity-recognition-ner .column-margin .term-gloss}
**named entity recognition (NER)** — finding the mentions of people,
organisations and places in text and saying which is which. The archetypal
sequence-labelling task, and the one this chapter measures.
[↩](#term-named-entity-recognition-ner){.term-back}
:::

The architecture is identical in all three: run the sentence through
something that produces one vector per token, put a classifier on top, read
off one label per token. That part is
[token classification](#gloss-token-classification){#term-token-classification .term-ref},
and it is genuinely the easy half.

::: {#gloss-token-classification .column-margin .term-gloss}
**token classification** — one label per token instead of one label per
document. The architecture NER, POS tagging and chunking all share; what
differs between them is the label set, not the model.
[↩](#term-token-classification){.term-back}
:::

The hard half is that [what you actually want is not labels, it is
spans]{.hl} — *"Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi is an organisation"*, not seven
separate token verdicts. Turning one into the other is a decoding problem,
and this chapter spends more time on decoding and measurement than on models,
because that is where the real defects are.

### The corpus

Everything in this chapter is measured on one dataset, so it is worth two
minutes of your attention before any of the numbers arrive.

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset("unimelb-nlp/wikiann", "tr")
```

```text
train        20,000 sentences   149,786 tokens   median length 6, mean 7.5
             26,482 entities    PER 8,833   ORG 7,970   LOC 9,679
validation   10,000 sentences    75,930 tokens
             13,517 entities    PER 4,374   ORG 4,129   LOC 5,014
test         10,000 sentences    75,731 tokens
             13,587 entities    PER 4,519   ORG 4,154   LOC 4,914
```

Three entity types, `PER`, `ORG` and `LOC`, and a striking absence: **every
sentence in this corpus contains at least one entity.** Real text does not
work that way — most sentences in a news feed or a ticket queue mention
nobody. Keep that in mind when you read the scores; it makes the task easier
than the one you will actually have.

### The floor, before anything else

@sec-classification insisted on computing the floor first, and the habit pays
here more dramatically than anywhere else in the book. A model that emits `O`
for every token — no features, no parameters, no training:

```text
everything-is-O      token accuracy 61.36%      span-level F1 0.00
```

[Sixty-one percent accurate, and it has never found a single
entity.]{.hl} The gap between those two numbers is not a curiosity; it is the
reason @sec-sequence-labeling-metrics exists. Any paper, model card or
colleague reporting "94% accuracy" on a tagging task is reporting a number
whose floor is 61.

**What we will look at.** First the corpus, audited before anything is
measured on it, because what that audit turns up changes how every later score
reads. Then the format that turns per-token labels into spans, and the
sequences a model emits that the format forbids. Then the alignment step
between words and subwords, where the silent bugs live. Then three ways of
building the thing — a dictionary, a CRF, a fine-tuned encoder — at six label
budgets, because the question is not which one wins but *when*. Then why the
metric everyone reports is the wrong one. And finally what happens if you skip
all of it and describe the schema to an LLM instead.

## What is actually in the corpus {#sec-sequence-labeling-audit}

@sec-data-annotation argued that you audit a labelled corpus before you
trust a number computed on it. WikiANN was built automatically, by
projecting Wikipedia's internal links through cross-lingual links
[@pan2017cross], which makes it enormous, free, available in 282 languages —
and unreviewed by anyone. So here is the audit.

It is not the first. @lignos2022meaningful examined WikiANN's contents for
lower-resourced languages and concluded that it overstates zero-shot
cross-lingual transfer; the point below is that argument re-run on Turkish, with
the numbers in front of you, plus one finding that neither the corpus paper nor
the audit paper prepares you for.

**These are mostly not sentences.**

```text
ends with . ! ?       6,896   34.5%
does not             13,104   65.5%
3 tokens or fewer       172    0.9%
```

Two thirds are fragments clipped out of Wikipedia markup. That is a fact about
the *domain*, and it will not transfer to prose.

**Some mentions are not mentions.**

```text
pure punctuation or digits    160   0.60%
containing wiki markup         63   0.24%

  ORG: '1966–67'
  ORG: '2012'
  ORG: '2013'
  ORG: '2000'
```

Bare years typed as organisations. A small fraction, but it puts a ceiling on
what any model can score, because some of the test set is simply wrong.

**The same string gets labelled two ways.**

```text
distinct surface forms                16,591
forms carrying more than one label       116   (0.7%)
mentions affected                      1,397   (5.3%)

  'Türkiye'      {LOC: 82, ORG: 4}
  'Almanya'      {LOC: 80, ORG:  2}
  'Fransa'       {LOC: 69, ORG:  5}
  'İtalya'       {LOC: 55, ORG:  1}
```

Some of this is real ambiguity — *Türkiye* beat *İtalya* is the football
federation, not the landmass — and some is annotation noise. Either way,
5.3% of mentions live in a class the model is being asked to guess.

### The part that changes how you read every score

Everything so far has been a nuisance: fragments instead of sentences, a
handful of bad labels, some ambiguity the model has to guess through. Annoying,
survivable, and roughly what you expect from an automatically built corpus.
This next one is a different kind of problem.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**13.06% of the test set is in the training set.**

```text
test sentences identical to a train sentence   1,306 / 10,000   13.06%
  of those, carrying an identical gold tagging  1,305
  carrying a different gold tagging                 1

validation sentences also in train             1,265   12.65%
test sentences also in validation                846    8.46%
duplicate sentences inside train itself        1,565
duplicate sentences inside test itself           540
```
:::

Not similar sentences. *Byte-identical token sequences* — compared on the token
lists exactly as `datasets` returns them, with no case folding, no Unicode
re-normalisation and no whitespace repair, so 13.06% is a lower bound on the
overlap rather than an upper one — 1,305 of them carrying byte-identical gold
labels. A model that does nothing but memorise
its training data gets those 1,306 sentences right for free.

This is the kind of thing @elangovan2021memorization warned about, and it is
worth being precise about who it flatters. Later in this chapter two systems
are scored separately on the leaked and the clean halves of the test set:

| system | leaked 1,306 | clean 8,694 | gap | gap / headroom |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Gazetteer (pure memorisation) | 77.54 | 51.04 | [+26.50]{.con} | 54% |
| CRF with hand features | **99.81** | 83.56 | [+16.25]{.con} | 99% |
| Fine-tuned BERTurk | 98.69 | 91.04 | [+7.65]{.pro} | 85% |

: Span-level F1, split by whether the test sentence was in training. The last
column divides the gap by the room the clean half left above it
{tbl-colwidths="[34,17,17,16,16]"}

The CRF scores **99.81** on the leaked half. It is not a better model there;
it is a lookup table that has seen the answer.

Read that gap column downwards, because it is the most useful thing in this
section. The three systems are ordered by how much they memorise — a
dictionary, a feature-based linear model, a pre-trained encoder — and the
leakage bonus falls with them in the same order: **+26.50, +16.25, +7.65**.

Read the last column too, though, because the raw gap is bounded above by
whatever headroom the clean half leaves: a system scoring 91.04 clean cannot
gain more than 8.96 no matter how much it memorises. Normalised, the ordering
reverses. The CRF's +16.25 uses **99%** of the 16.44 points available to it; the
gazetteer's larger +26.50 uses only **54%** of its 48.96. The two readings agree
on the practical point and disagree on the ranking, which is exactly why the gap
is a **diagnostic rather than a memorisation score**: a large gap means look
harder, not that you have measured how much your model memorises. Three systems
on one corpus is as far as this evidence goes.

What both readings do support: a benchmark with 13% leakage does not just
inflate scores. It inflates them *unevenly*, and the systems it flatters most
are the ones that will disappoint you in production.

One number in that table deserves a second look before you read the gap column
at all. A dictionary that has memorised every training string ought to score
near 100 on sentences it has seen verbatim, and it scores 77.54. The missing
twenty-two points are the two nuisances from earlier in this section arriving
together: longest match fires on strings that are entities *somewhere* in
training but not here, and when a surface form carries two labels — the 5.3% of
mentions in the table above — the dictionary has to pick one. Even pure
memorisation does not get a leaked test set for free. It just gets most of it.

Every headline number in this chapter is computed on the full test set,
because that is what the literature reports and comparisons have to be
like-for-like. But the clean-half column is the one to believe.

::: {.column-margin}
The honest fix is to deduplicate against training before scoring, and to say
so. The cheaper habit, and the one worth carrying out of this chapter: when a
result looks too good, hash your test inputs and check how many of them your
model has already seen. It takes four lines and it has saved more projects
than any modelling trick in this book.
:::

## Tagging schemes and span decoding {#sec-sequence-labeling-bio}

A tagger emits one label per token. You want spans. The bridge is a *tagging
scheme*, and the standard one is
[BIO](#gloss-bio-tagging){#term-bio-tagging .term-ref}: `B-X` opens a span of
type X, `I-X` continues it, `O` is everything else.

One clarification before the grammar, because it decides what counts as
illegal. The scheme this chapter uses — and the one `datasets` ships WikiANN
in — is **IOB2**: every span opens with `B-`, without exception. The original
CoNLL-2003 scheme, usually called IOB1, is a different thing: there `B-`
appears *only* to separate two adjacent spans of the same type, so a span
normally opens with `I-` and `O → I-PER` is perfectly legal. Everything below
about forbidden transitions is a statement about IOB2. Run an
illegal-transition counter over CoNLL-2003 as distributed and it will report
thousands of violations that are not violations.

::: {#gloss-bio-tagging .column-margin .term-gloss}
**BIO tagging** — `B-` marks a span's first token, `I-` a continuation, `O`
everything outside. The trick that lets a per-token classifier express
multi-token spans, including two of the same type back to back.
[↩](#term-bio-tagging){.term-back}
:::

::::

The `B`/`I` distinction is not decoration. Without it, two adjacent entities
of the same type would merge into one: `Ali` `Veli` as `PER PER` is one span
or two, and you cannot tell. With BIO, `B-PER B-PER` is unambiguously two.

BIOES adds `E-` for the last token of a span and `S-` for a single-token
span. It gives the model more specific classes to learn and the decoder more
redundancy to check, at the cost of nearly doubling the label set.
@ratinov2009design compared them carefully and found BIOES ahead on their
setup — which is worth knowing mostly so you can say *it depends on the
corpus* with a citation behind it, rather than repeating whichever one your
first tutorial used.

### The sequences that should not exist {#sec-sequence-labeling-illegal}

BIO has grammar. `I-PER` may follow `B-PER` or `I-PER`. It may not follow
`O`, and it may not follow `B-LOC`. A tagger that scores each token
independently does not know that.

Here is how often the gold data and three systems break the rule, across the
10,000 test sentences:

```text
                              I- after O    I- after a different type
gold test set                          0                            0
gazetteer (longest match)              0                            0
CRF                                    0                            0
fine-tuned BERTurk                    49                           90
```

[The CRF emitted no illegal transition at any budget; the fine-tuned
transformer — the best model in this chapter, at 91.92 span F1 — emits 139 of
them.]{.hl} Read the CRF's zero as measured, not as guaranteed: an ordinary CRF
learns *finite* transition scores, so it can only make an invalid transition
expensive, never impossible. Ruling one out takes a hard constraint, which is
the next section. That
inversion surprises people, and the reason is structural rather than a matter
of quality.

A softmax tagger picks the highest-scoring label at each position
*independently*. Nothing in the arithmetic couples position 4 to position 5,
so `O` followed by `I-ORG` is available whenever the scores happen to favour
it. A [CRF](#gloss-crf){.term-ref}
[@lafferty2001crf] scores whole *sequences*: it learns a transition score for
every label pair it saw in training and leaves the pairs it never saw —
`O → I-ORG` among them — without a supporting feature at all. (That is
CRFsuite's default; `feature.possible_transitions` turns it off, and the
consequence is that an unseen transition scores 0 rather than being
penalised — it is simply outbid by the legal ones.) Then
[Viterbi decoding](#gloss-viterbi-decoding){#term-viterbi-decoding .term-ref} [@viterbi1967error]
returns the best-scoring *path* rather than the best label at each step, so an
illegal transition has to pay for itself out of the emission scores of the
whole rest of the sentence. It never does: across 10,000 test sentences and
every label budget in this chapter, the CRF emitted zero. **That is a measured
outcome, not a theorem.** The scores are finite, so the path is improbable
rather than impossible; if you need the guarantee instead of the empirical
zero, the next subsection is how to get it.

::: {#gloss-viterbi-decoding .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Viterbi decoding** — a dynamic program that finds the single
highest-scoring label sequence, instead of taking the best label at each
position separately. What lets a CRF price a forbidden transition against the
whole sentence rather than against one token.
[↩](#term-viterbi-decoding){.term-back}
:::

::: {.column-margin}
This is exactly why the classic neural NER architecture was BiLSTM-**CRF**
[@lample2016neural] rather than BiLSTM alone: the encoder supplies the
features, the CRF layer supplies the grammar. Whether that layer still earns
its cost on top of a transformer is an open question this chapter does not
settle: @sec-sequence-labeling-encoder measures the plain softmax head only.
The transition mask below is the cheap alternative to finding out.
:::

### What a decoder does with a broken sequence

So your model emits `O I-ORG I-ORG`. What is that? There is no right answer,
only conventions, and they disagree:

| decoder | `O I-ORG I-ORG` becomes | rationale |
|:--|:--|:--|
| lenient (`seqeval`, `conlleval` [@tjongkimsang2003conll]) | one `ORG` span over tokens 2–3 | a stray `I-` opens a span; recover what you can |
| strict | nothing | the sequence is invalid; refuse to guess |
| repair-then-decode | rewrite to `O B-ORG I-ORG`, then decode | fix the grammar first, score after |

: Three readings of the same predictions {tbl-colwidths="[26,32,42]"}

The point is not which to pick. The point is that [your reported F1 depends
on a decoder you probably did not choose deliberately]{.hl}, and the
difference is invisible unless you look for it. On the CRF's predictions the
choice happens to cost nothing, because there is nothing to disagree about:

```text
same CRF predictions, two decoders
  lenient (a stray I- opens a span)    F1 85.45
  strict  (a stray I- is dropped)      F1 85.45
```

On the transformer's 139 malformed transitions it would not be a tie. When
you compare your numbers against a paper's, the decoder is one of the things
that has to match.

### Making the grammar structural instead of learned

You do not have to add a CRF layer to get the well-formedness a learned model
only supplies empirically. A transition mask over the softmax logits, decoded
with Viterbi, gives it at inference time — no extra parameters, no retraining.
One note on the constant below: $-10^4$ is a large finite penalty rather than
$-\infty$, which keeps the arithmetic well behaved in the training objective —
$-\infty$ is fine inside a log-sum-exp on its own, since
$\log(e^{-\infty} + e^{0}) = 0$, and turns into `nan` only when every path
through a position is impossible or when the gradient touches it. It makes an
illegal path lose in any realistic score range; it does not make it
mathematically impossible. If you want the true constraint, remove
the invalid transitions and start states from the search space rather than
pricing them.

``` python
import torch

NEG = -1e4
mask = torch.zeros(L, L)                    # L = number of labels
for a, la in enumerate(labels):
    for b, lb in enumerate(labels):
        if lb.startswith("I-"):             # I-X may only follow B-X or I-X
            if la not in (f"B-{lb[2:]}", f"I-{lb[2:]}"):
                mask[a, b] = NEG

def viterbi(logits, mask):                  # logits: (T, L) log-probabilities
    dp, bp = logits[0].clone(), []
    for t in range(1, logits.shape[0]):
        score = dp[:, None] + mask + logits[t][None, :]
        dp, best = score.max(0)
        bp.append(best)
    path = [int(dp.argmax())]
    for back in reversed(bp):
        path.append(int(back[path[-1]]))
    return list(reversed(path))
```

That took the 139 illegal transitions to 0 in this run, for the price of a
matrix and a dynamic program. Not by construction: a finite penalty is still a
price, and an emission score large enough would still buy an illegal step. Drop
the invalid entries from the search space instead of pricing them and the
guarantee is real. Whether it *helps* is a separate
question and one you should measure on your own schema rather than assume: it
converts malformed spans into well-formed ones, and the lenient decoder was
already recovering some of them. We did not run that comparison, which is the
gap this subsection leaves open — but the mask is what to reach for before an
extra trained layer.

## The subword alignment trap {#sec-sequence-labeling-alignment}

Your labels are per *word*. A transformer's inputs are per *subword*. Every
sequence-labelling pipeline therefore contains an alignment step, and it is
the single most common place to introduce a silent bug — silent because the
model still trains, the loss still falls, and the score is merely worse than
it should be.

Turkish makes the problem vivid. Here is BERTurk's tokenizer on entity words
from this corpus:

```text
Türkiye'nin      -> ['Türkiye', "'", 'nin']
Takımı'nı        -> ['Takımı', "'", 'nı']
Mississippi'de   -> ['Miss', '##iss', '##ip', '##pi', "'", 'de']
Baudelaire'in    -> ['Ba', '##ude', '##la', '##ire', "'", 'in']
Erdemir          -> ['Erdem', '##ir']
İstanbul         -> ['İstanbul']
```

One word, six subwords. And the fragmentation is not evenly spread — it
concentrates on exactly the words you are trying to label:

```text
BERTurk (dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased)
  entity words   1.98 subwords/word   53.8% split into more than one piece
  other words    1.45 subwords/word   30.9% split
  -> entity words are 1.36x more fragmented

mBERT (bert-base-multilingual-cased)
  entity words   1.90 subwords/word   47.3% split
  other words    2.00 subwords/word   45.5% split
```

Names are rarer than common words, so the tokenizer has less reason to keep
them whole — the mechanism @sec-text-as-data described, arriving here as a
concrete cost.

The mBERT row is worth reading carefully, because it is easy to over-read. It
fragments *everything* in Turkish at 2.00 subwords per word, which is
@sec-pretraining's argument for language-specific tokenizers: more tokens for
the same text means more cost and less effective context, permanently.

What it is **not** is evidence that mBERT will score worse on this task.
Tokenization is what was measured here; accuracy is not. @sec-turkish-nlp
fine-tunes both models on this exact dataset and finds the multilingual one
slightly *ahead* — a useful reminder that a tokenizer tax is a tax on tokens
rather than a prediction about F1.

### The alignment itself

The convention is to label the **first** subword of each word and mask the
rest with `-100`, the index PyTorch's cross-entropy ignores. Here is that
convention on three of the entity words above — and, underneath it, what
happens when you skip the alignment and zip the labels on by position.

::: {.fig-cap}
The three tokenizations are BERTurk's, printed verbatim above. Nothing
connects the rows except the columns: each word sits over exactly the subwords
it was split into, which is what `word_ids()` gives you and what a positional
zip throws away.
:::
::::

In code:

```python
enc = tok(batch["tokens"], is_split_into_words=True, truncation=True)

labels = []
for i, tags in enumerate(batch["ner_tags"]):
    word_ids = enc.word_ids(batch_index=i)
    prev, row = None, []
    for wid in word_ids:
        if wid is None:            # [CLS], [SEP], padding
            row.append(-100)
        elif wid != prev:          # first subword of a word: label it
            row.append(tags[wid])
        else:                      # continuation: ignore in the loss
            row.append(-100)
        prev = wid
    labels.append(row)
```

Three ways this goes wrong, all of which still run:

1. **Forgetting `word_ids()` and zipping labels to subwords positionally.**
   The moment any word splits, every subsequent label is attached to the
   wrong token. With 53.8% of entity words splitting, the labels are
   scrambled almost immediately. Training proceeds; F1 lands somewhere near
   noise.
2. **Propagating the word's label to every subword.** Defensible, and
   sometimes done — but if you propagate `B-PER` rather than converting
   continuations to `I-PER`, you have taught the model that a person's name
   starts four times.
3. **Forgetting that `[CLS]` and `[SEP]` exist.** An off-by-one that shifts
   every label by one position.

[If a sequence-labelling model scores far below expectation, check the
alignment before you touch the model.]{.hl} Print one tokenized sentence
beside its aligned labels and read it. It takes a minute and it is the
highest-yield minute in this chapter.

## Baselines before transformers {#sec-sequence-labeling-baselines}

@sec-classification's discipline: build the cheap thing first, and make the
expensive thing beat it.

### A gazetteer

Memorise every entity string in the training data, then tag test sentences by
longest match. No learning, no features, no generalisation whatsoever.

```text
gazetteer (16,591 memorised phrases, longest match)
  token accuracy 75.73%
  span   P 59.73   R 51.41   F1 55.26      (0.1s to tag 10,000 sentences)
```

Fifty-five F1 from a Python dictionary. That is the number a model has to
justify itself against, and it is higher than most people guess — because
names repeat. In this corpus [52.2% of test mentions appear verbatim in the
training data]{.hl}, which is simultaneously the gazetteer's ceiling on
recall and a restatement of the leakage problem from
@sec-sequence-labeling-audit.

::: {#gloss-gazetteer .column-margin .term-gloss}
**gazetteer** — a memorised list of known entity strings, matched against
text directly. Fast, exact, completely unable to recognise a name it has
never seen. [↩](#term-gazetteer){.term-back}
:::

A [gazetteer](#gloss-gazetteer){#term-gazetteer .term-ref} is also the right
answer more often than its reputation suggests. If your entities are a
closed set — the parts in your catalogue, the drugs in a formulary, the 81
provinces of Turkey — then the list *is* the ground truth and a model can
only approximate it.

### A CRF

The gazetteer cannot recognise a name it has never seen, because it has no
notion of what a name *looks like*. So give a model that notion by hand.
Capitalisation, suffixes, the shape of the word, what its neighbours look like.

A linear-chain [CRF](#gloss-crf){#term-crf .term-ref} scores a whole label
sequence $y = (y_1, \dots, y_T)$ for a sentence $x$ as a sum of two kinds of
term — one that looks at the token, one that looks at the label pair:

$$
s(x, y) \;=\; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \underbrace{\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{f}(x, t, y_t)}_{\text{emission}}
           \;+\; \sum_{t=2}^{T} \underbrace{A_{y_{t-1},\, y_t}}_{\text{transition}}
$$

and turns that score into a probability by normalising over *every* label
sequence, which is what makes it a model of the sequence rather than of each
token:

$$
p(y \mid x) \;=\; \frac{\exp s(x, y)}{\sum_{y'} \exp s(x, y')}
$$

Two things follow from that denominator. Training maximises the log-likelihood
of the gold sequence — the `c1` and `c2` in the code below are $L_1$ and $L_2$
penalties on $\mathbf{w}$ and $A$ — and prediction takes
$\arg\max_y s(x, y)$, which Viterbi computes in $O(T L^2)$ instead of the
$L^T$ the sum suggests.

The name for what the conditioning buys is worth having. A hidden Markov model
is **generative**: it models the joint $p(x, y)$, so it has to describe how the
*words* were produced, and that forces strong independence assumptions on
them — you cannot casually add "the previous word is title-cased" and "this
word ends in *-nin*" as overlapping evidence without the model double-counting.
A CRF is **discriminative**: it models $p(y \mid x)$ directly and never has to
explain where $x$ came from, so the feature dictionary below can contain
whatever correlated, hand-designed, overlapping signals you like. That freedom
is the whole reason the feature template is written by hand, and the reason a
CRF beat the alternatives on this shape of task in 2001 [@lafferty2001crf].

::: {#gloss-crf .column-margin .term-gloss}
**conditional random field (CRF)** — a discriminative model that scores a whole
label sequence at once, adding a learned transition score for each adjacent
label pair to the per-token feature scores. Models $p(y \mid x)$ rather than
$p(x, y)$, which is what lets its features overlap freely.
[↩](#term-crf){.term-back}
:::

Over twenty thousand sentences:

```python
def features(tokens, i):
    w = tokens[i]
    f = {
        "bias": 1.0,
        "w.lower": w.lower(),
        "w[-3:]": w[-3:], "w[-2:]": w[-2:],        # Turkish suffixes
        "w.isupper": w.isupper(), "w.istitle": w.istitle(),
        "w.isdigit": w.isdigit(),
        "w.hasapos": ("'" in w or "’" in w),        # Türkiye'nin
        "w.shape": shape(w),                        # Xxxxx, 9999
        "w.len": min(len(w), 12),
    }
    for off in (-2, -1, 1, 2):                      # a window of context
        j = i + off
        if 0 <= j < len(tokens):
            v = tokens[j]
            f[f"{off:+d}:w.lower"] = v.lower()
            f[f"{off:+d}:w.istitle"] = v.istitle()
            f[f"{off:+d}:w[-3:]"] = v[-3:]
        else:
            f[f"{off:+d}:BOS_EOS"] = True
    return f
```

```text
CRF (sklearn-crfsuite, lbfgs, c1=0.1, c2=0.1, 200 iterations)
  fit 18.5s        predict 0.2s for 10,000 sentences

  token accuracy 94.41%      token-level micro-F1 88.73
  span   P 86.27   R 84.64   F1 85.45      macro-F1 85.34

     PER   P 88.64   R 88.56   F1 88.60    (n=4,519)
     LOC   P 84.09   R 86.06   F1 85.06    (n=4,914)
     ORG   P 86.34   R 78.70   F1 82.34    (n=4,154)
```

**85.45 span F1 in eighteen seconds on a CPU.** No GPU, no pre-training, no
downloads. This is the number the rest of the chapter has to beat, and it is
a genuinely hard target.

Two things in that table are worth reading rather than skimming. `ORG` recall
is 78.70, seven points below `PER` — organisations are long, compositional
and open-ended (*Slovenya Millî Basketbol Takımı*), so a five-token window
sees only part of one. And the `w.hasapos` feature is doing real work: in
Turkish an apostrophe is a reliable signal that the preceding characters are
a proper noun, which is a piece of orthographic luck other languages do not
get.

## Fine-tuning an encoder {#sec-sequence-labeling-encoder}

Same task, same test set, `AutoModelForTokenClassification` on top of
BERTurk, first-subword alignment as above, three epochs, learning rate 3e-5.
The interesting question is not "does it win" but "at what label budget does
it start winning", so the run is a curve rather than a point.

```text
budget    token acc   span P   span R   span F1   macro   illegal   train s
   200        63.43     9.02     1.90      3.14    2.95      1561       5.6
   500        85.04    51.25    58.11     54.47   54.05      3739      12.6
 1,000        92.59    74.99    80.44     77.62   77.26       915      24.6
 2,000        94.68    82.74    85.78     84.23   84.04       538      48.9
 5,000        95.96    87.44    89.24     88.33   88.16       304     121.3
20,000        97.20    91.49    92.35     91.92   91.82       139     476.6

CRF, all 20,000 sentences   94.41    86.27    84.64     85.45   85.34    0    18.5
```

**One run per budget, seed 42, no hyper-parameter search — and the two small
budgets are the volatile ones.** At 200 sentences whether a randomly initialised
head escapes the all-`O` solution at all is close to a coin flip across seeds,
so read 3.14 as *single digits* rather than as a number with two decimals behind
it. There is also a floor under every comparison in this table: span F1 near 85%
over the test set's 13,587 gold spans carries a 95% interval of roughly
$\pm 0.6$ points, so the 84.23-against-85.45 comparison that fixes the crossover
is a gap of about two standard errors, not a settled fact. Three seeds per budget
is the measurement this table is missing.

At the full budget the encoder reaches **91.92 span F1** against the CRF's
85.45 — six and a half points, for 477 seconds of GPU training instead of 18
seconds of CPU, and 10.3 seconds of inference over the test set instead of
0.2.

Read the top row again. [At 200 labelled sentences, a fine-tuned transformer
scores 3.14 span F1 — while a dictionary of memorised strings scores
55.26.]{.hl}

That is not a bug, and it is the most useful thing in this chapter. At 200
sentences the model has seen roughly 265 entities spread over six entity tags
plus `O`; the classification head is randomly initialised; and at batch size 16,
three epochs is **39 gradient updates**.

Note what that last number does to the diagnosis. Every row in this table uses
the same three epochs at 3e-5 — a schedule tuned for the full budget, which
starves the small ones. So some of that 3.14 is the label budget and some of it
is the schedule, and this run does not separate them. The standard remedy at 200
examples is ten to twenty epochs, possibly at a higher learning rate; running
that is the first thing to try before drawing the conclusion, and we did not.
The conclusion survives the doubt — nothing about a longer schedule closes a
fifty-point gap to a dictionary — but the raw number is a schedule artefact as
much as a data-budget one.

Token accuracy is 63.43% — barely above the everything-is-`O` floor of
61.36% — which tells you precisely what it learned. It learned to say `O`. It
picks up almost no entities at all (recall 1.90), and the few it does are
mostly wrong.

The crossover against the CRF sits between **2,000 and 5,000** labelled
sentences: at 2,000 the encoder is still a point behind (84.23 against
85.45), and by 5,000 it is nearly three ahead. So [somewhere around two and a
half thousand labelled sentences of BERTurk buy what twenty thousand
sentences of hand-engineered CRF buy]{.hl} — call it a fourfold to tenfold
reduction in annotation, which is the range the measured crossover actually
supports and the honest case for pre-training on this
task, and smaller than the folklore suggests. Be exact about what that
comparison is: a **label-efficiency** claim, in which the encoder's budget
varies while the CRF's stays at 20,000. It is not a claim that the encoder wins
at a matched budget — at a matched 2,000 sentences the CRF is the one in front
in the row above. Below that crossover the
classical pipeline is not a fallback; it is the better model.

The `illegal` column is worth a second look, because it says something the F1
column does not. Well-formedness is *learned* here, not guaranteed: illegal
BIO transitions peak at 3,739 once the model starts emitting entity tags at
all, then fall steadily as it picks up the grammar from data.

And they never reach zero. Even at 20,000 sentences and 91.92 F1, the tagger
emits 139 sequences that IOB2 forbids. The CRF emitted none at any budget,
because Viterbi prices the whole sequence and a transition with no supporting
feature never earns its place in the winning path. If you want the guarantee
rather than the empirical zero, mask the forbidden transitions before decoding
(@sec-sequence-labeling-bio).

::: {.column-margin}
Notice which way the errors run. The CRF is precision-leaning (86.27 P
against 84.64 R); every encoder row from 500 up is recall-leaning. Feature
templates fire when they match and stay silent otherwise, while a fine-tuned
encoder will guess. Which failure you prefer is a product decision, and
@sec-classification-costs is the machinery for making it.
:::

:::

## Token accuracy is the wrong metric {#sec-sequence-labeling-metrics}

Three numbers, all computed on the same CRF predictions over the same 10,000
test sentences:

```text
token accuracy                94.41
token-level micro-F1          88.73      (entity tags only, O excluded)
span-level F1                 85.45      (exact match on type, start and end)
```

They differ because they ask different questions, and only the last one asks
the question you care about.

**Token accuracy** counts every token, including the 61% that are `O`.
Predicting `O` everywhere already scores 61.36, so the informative range of
this metric is the thirty-odd points between 61 and the low 90s — and it gets
worse, not better, on realistic corpora where most sentences contain no
entity at all. It is the metric that makes a model look finished when it is
not.

**Token-level F1 over entity tags** drops the `O` class, which fixes the
floor. But it still gives partial credit: get three tokens of a four-token
organisation right and you score three quarters of a hit. No downstream
system can use three quarters of an organisation name.

**[Span-level F1](#gloss-span-level-f1){#term-span-level-f1 .term-ref}**
requires the type, the start and the end to all be right. It is the only one
of the three that corresponds to "did we extract the record correctly", which
is why it is what NER papers report.

Two independent choices hide inside the phrase "span-level F1", and separating
them saves an argument later. **Exact match** is about boundaries: does the
predicted span's type, start and end all match a gold span? **Strict versus
lenient** is about what the decoder does with a malformed tag sequence *before*
any matching happens. `seqeval` is exact-match in both of its modes; its default
mode is the lenient one, and `mode="strict", scheme=IOB2` is the other.

::: {.column-margin}
**Every span-level number in this chapter is computed in the lenient
convention** — `seqeval`'s default, and `conlleval`'s.
The scorer used throughout this chapter is written out rather than imported,
so that the decoding it assumes is visible. It was checked against `seqeval`
on deliberately corrupted predictions and agrees to four decimal places —
P 46.2332, R 75.2042, F1 57.2629 from both. If you write your own, run that
comparison; the disagreements are always in the malformed sequences.
:::

::: {#gloss-span-level-f1 .column-margin .term-gloss}
**span-level F1** — a prediction counts as correct only if its type, its
first token and its last token all match a gold span. Partial overlaps score
zero, which is the point: half an entity is not half useful.
[↩](#term-span-level-f1){.term-back}
:::

Most of the gap between token-level 88.73 and span-level 85.45 is boundary errors — spans where the type was right and an edge was wrong. (The two metrics also weight spans differently, so the gap is not a pure error count.)
Turkish makes those common, for a reason worth naming: the boundary of a
Turkish entity is frequently *inside* an orthographic word, because the
suffix that marks the case is attached to the name.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## When partial credit is the right call

Exact match is the convention, not a law. If your downstream consumer is a
human reviewing highlighted text, a span that is off by one token is nearly
as useful as a perfect one, and reporting only exact match will make you
reject models your users would have preferred.

The alternatives are the MUC-style partial-credit schemes [@chinchor1993muc]
and the entity-type
/ partial / exact breakdown that `nervaluate` implements. Use them when they
match your consumer, and *say which you used* — a paper reporting 90 under
partial credit is not beating a paper reporting 88 under exact match.
:::

### Where the errors are

A single F1 number tells you how much is wrong and nothing about what. Split
it by entity type and the same two systems look rather different:

```text
                CRF                       BERTurk @ 20,000
        precision  recall      F1     precision  recall      F1   support
  PER       88.64   88.56   88.60         94.19   94.73   94.46     4,519
  LOC       84.09   86.06   85.06         91.16   93.22   92.18     4,914
  ORG       86.34   78.70   82.34         88.93   88.73   88.83     4,154
```

`ORG` is last in both columns, and its recall is the outlier — 78.70 for the
CRF, and still the lowest of the three at 88.73 for the encoder six points
further up. Six points of extra model did not move `ORG` off the bottom.

The reason is in the spans themselves. Organisation names are long — mean
gold span **2.68 tokens for `ORG` against 2.26 for `PER` and 1.61 for
`LOC`** — compositional, and frequently built out of ordinary words
(*Türk Silahlı Kuvvetleri*, *Eurovision Şarkı Yarışması*). A model with a
five-token window structurally cannot see all of one, and a model that can
still has to decide where it stops.

Report macro-F1 alongside micro when your types are this uneven. Here they
are close (85.34 macro against 85.45 micro) only because the three types
happen to be similarly sized; in a schema with one rare type and one common
one they diverge sharply, exactly as @sec-classification showed for document
labels.

**One boundary on all of this, since the chapter opened with three tasks and
measured one.** Everything above about spans, BIO and span-level F1 applies to
tasks whose output is a *span*: NER, chunking, slot filling. POS tagging is not
one of them — every token carries a label, no token is `O`, and there is nothing
to decode — so token accuracy is a perfectly reasonable metric there, and its
floor is the most-frequent-tag baseline (around 90% on most treebanks) rather
than 61%. The architecture is shared; the evaluation is not. If you came here
for POS on Turkish, the label set is Universal Dependencies' and the corpora are
the UD Turkish treebanks (BOUN, IMST) — but @sec-sequence-labeling-alignment is
the part of this chapter you still need, because the subword problem does not
care what the labels mean.

## Schema-guided extraction with an LLM {#sec-sequence-labeling-llm}

The 2026 alternative to training a tagger is to describe the schema and ask.
No labelled data, no training run, an afternoon of prompt iteration. It works
well enough to be a real option and it fails in ways a tagger never does, so
it needs measuring rather than believing.

The setup is deliberately favourable: the annotation guidelines go in the
prompt, the output is constrained to a JSON schema, temperature is 0.

```python
SCHEMA = {
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "entities": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "text": {"type": "string"},
          "type": {"type": "string", "enum": ["PER", "ORG", "LOC"]},
        },
        "required": ["text", "type"],
      },
    }
  },
  "required": ["entities"],
}
```

### The trap that costs a day

Before any results, a bug worth more than the results. The same schema, the
same model, the same server — two endpoints:

```text
POST /api/generate   with format=<schema>
  -> {"answer": 1}

POST /api/chat       with format=<schema>
  -> "The capital of France is **Paris**.\n\nLocated in the north-central
      part of the country along the Seine River, Paris is..."
```

The schema said the reply must be an object with an integer `answer`. On
`/api/generate` the constraint was enforced. On `/api/chat`, with `ollama`
0.24.0 on Apple Silicon and thinking disabled, [the `format` field was silently
ignored]{.hl} and the model returned prose. No error, no warning, no field in
the response saying the constraint had been dropped.

Be careful which variable you blame, though, because we did not isolate it.
This is a known *class* of bug rather than a property of `/api/chat`: the
upstream tracker carries several reports of `format` being dropped without
warning, and they point at the runner and the flags rather than at the
endpoint — one backend dropping the constraint while a different build of the
same model enforces it, and `think: false` disabling it on some models. Our
setup sits at exactly that intersection. The lesson survives either
diagnosis, and it is the practical one: pin your server version, and assume
the constraint is off until a request has proved it is on.

Run that inside an extraction pipeline with a `try/except json.JSONDecodeError`
around the parse, and you get an extractor that returns zero entities for every
document and a metrics table full of zeros you will spend an afternoon
blaming on your prompt.

::: {.column-margin}
Note also *what* the constrained call returned: `{"answer": 1}`. Paris is not
an integer, so grammar-constrained decoding produced something schema-valid
and semantically worthless. [A schema guarantees shape, never
truth.]{.hl} @sec-decoding is where the machinery behind this lives — how
grammars constrain sampling, and what they cost.
:::

The general rule this stands for: **verify that your structured-output
constraint is actually being applied, by sending one request whose schema the
model would otherwise violate.** A schema you believe is enforced and is not
is worse than no schema, because it removes the malformed output that would
have told you.

### Getting the answer back onto the text

A tagger returns positions. An LLM returns *strings*. Nothing in
`{"text": "Samsun", "type": "LOC"}` says which tokens that was, and span-level
F1 is defined over token offsets — so every LLM answer has to be aligned back
onto the sentence before it can be scored at all.

This step is usually skipped in write-ups and it is where the interesting
failures are:

```python
def align_span(tokens, text):
    want = text.split()
    for i in range(len(tokens) - len(want) + 1):      # 1. exact token run
        if tokens[i:i + len(want)] == want:
            return i, i + len(want)
    ...                                               # 2. ignore whitespace
    ...                                               # 3. allow a dropped suffix
    return None                                       # not in the sentence
```

Three things can come back:

- **A mention that is there** — align it, score it.
- **A mention with the Turkish suffix stripped.** The model returns `Samsun`;
  the token is `Samsun'a`. The guidelines asked for an exact copy and it
  helpfully normalised. Fallback 3 exists for this and it is doing real work.
- **A mention that is not in the sentence at all.** A paraphrase, an
  expansion, an inference. There is no honest way to score it, and counting
  it as a hit would be scoring the model on a claim about text it invented.

It is tempting to call every unalignable mention a hallucination and move on.
That turns out to be mostly wrong, and finding out why is worth the section.

Across 1,000 sentences the model returned **1,419 typed mentions**, of which
31 would not align. Sorting those 31 by cause:

```text
aligned directly                              1,388   97.82%
recovered by normalising apostrophes              7    0.49%   ' vs ’
recovered by stripping wiki markup               20    1.41%   ''Gorran ''
genuinely not in the sentence                     4    0.28%
```

[Twenty-seven of the thirty-one failures were the aligner's fault, not the
model's.]{.hl} Twenty came from the corpus's own Wikipedia markup, seven from
the model normalising a curly apostrophe to a straight one. Had this been
reported without looking, the headline would have been "the model hallucinated
31 entities" — a claim about the model that is really a claim about
preprocessing.

And the second half of the lesson, which is less comfortable: fixing the
aligner **barely moves the score**, from 60.57 to 60.29 F1. Recall rises
(60.82 to 61.11) and precision falls (60.33 to 59.50), because the recovered
mentions were mostly wrong anyway. So check the alignment — and do not expect
it to be the explanation for a disappointing number.

The four genuinely unalignable mentions are all suffix-boundary confusions
rather than invention: the model returned `Çin Halk Cumhuriyeti` where the
text has `Çin Halk Cumhuriyetini` with the accusative fused on and no
apostrophe to split at, and `Niksar'ın` where the text has `Niksar'da` — the
right name, the wrong case.

### The results

Same 1,000 test sentences for every system, 1,373 gold entities, scored the
same way:

| system | labels used | token acc | span P | span R | span F1 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Gazetteer | 20,000 sentences | 76.12 | 60.28 | 50.40 | 54.90 |
| **LLM, zero-shot** | **none** | 82.87 | 60.33 | 60.82 | **60.57** |
| CRF | 20,000 sentences | 94.42 | 84.94 | 83.39 | 84.16 |
| BERTurk fine-tuned | 20,000 sentences | 96.98 | 91.11 | 91.77 | **91.44** |

: `qwen3.5:9b` against the taggers, on the identical slice. The LLM row uses the
*naive* aligner; the corrected one scores 60.29
{tbl-colwidths="[26,20,14,13,13,14]"}

Note which of the two numbers is in that row, because a chapter about auditing
should not quote the flattering one silently. 60.57 comes from the aligner
before the apostrophe and wiki-markup fixes; the corrected aligner gives 60.29.
The gap is 0.28 and changes nothing here — but that is exactly the situation in
which a headline number gets carried forward without anyone checking which
alignment produced it.

Two readings, and both matter.

**With no training data at all, the LLM beats the gazetteer by six points.**
That is a real capability and it did not exist in 2019. If you have a schema
and no labels, this is a working extractor by tomorrow.

**It also loses to an eighteen-second CRF by 24 points, and to the fine-tuned
encoder by 31.** Zero-shot extraction is where you *start*, not where you
stop, and the gap is far larger than the marketing around structured output
suggests.

The per-type breakdown says where it goes wrong:

```text
             LLM              BERTurk @ 20,000
        P      R     F1        P      R     F1
  PER 64.63  82.00  72.29    92.97  95.32  94.13
  LOC 59.01  59.24  59.13    92.12  93.93  93.02
  ORG 54.67  40.10  46.26    90.46  87.97  89.20
```

`ORG` recall of **40.10** is the headline failure: the model misses three
organisations in five. This is the same weakness every system in this chapter
has, amplified — but it also has a cause the taggers do not share. The model
is not failing to *find* the strings; it is disagreeing about whether
*Değişim Hareketi* is an organisation, and about where its name stops. A
tagger learns that boundary convention from 20,000 examples of it. A prompt
has to state it, and one page of guidelines cannot encode what annotators
converged on over a corpus.

`PER` shows the mirror image: recall 82.00 against precision 64.63. The model
finds people eagerly and over-commits, tagging descriptions and titles that
the guidelines exclude.

### What it costs

So far the LLM has been judged on accuracy alone, where it lost by 31 points.
The second axis is worse for it, and by a margin that is easy to
underestimate until you see it written down:

```text
                              LLM (qwen3.5:9b)     BERTurk fine-tuned
per sentence                        1.26 s              0.00103 s
1,000 sentences                    1,265 s                    1.0 s
generated tokens per sentence          26.4                    n/a
malformed JSON responses                  0
```

[The LLM is roughly 1,200 times slower per sentence]{.hl} — and that is a
9B model quantised to 4 bits, running locally, with thinking disabled and a
schema that keeps the output to 26 tokens. A hosted frontier model would be
more accurate and no faster.

For a thousand documents that difference is nothing. For the ten million
documents an extraction pipeline usually has to get through, 1.26 seconds
each is 146 days of wall clock. The decision rule from
@sec-classification-crossover applies unchanged: prompt at low volume,
distil into a tagger when the volume arrives.

::: {.column-margin}
The right middle option is missing from that table on purpose, because it
deserves naming rather than a row: **use the LLM to label, then train the
tagger on its output.** At 60.57 F1 the model is a poor extractor and a
serviceable annotator — it gives you thousands of noisy labels overnight,
which @sec-sequence-labeling-encoder's curve says is exactly the regime where
a fine-tuned encoder starts to work. @sec-data-annotation is the chapter on
doing that without fooling yourself.
:::

### The option this section skipped

The comparison above is between a *general-purpose* LLM and a *trained* tagger,
and it leaves out the family built precisely for the gap between them. GLiNER
[@zaratiana2024gliner] is a BERT-sized encoder trained to match free-form type
*names* against candidate spans, so it does zero-shot extraction over an
arbitrary label set at encoder latency rather than generation latency.
UniversalNER [@zhou2024universalner] takes the instruction-tuned route to the
same target, and NuNER [@bogdanov2024nuner] pre-trains a 125M encoder on
LLM-generated annotations. Published comparisons put a 90M GLiNER in the same
zero-shot range as a 13B UniversalNER.

So the honest shape of the zero-label decision is three options, not two:

| option | labels | latency | when |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| prompt an LLM under a schema | none | ~1.3 s/sentence | prototyping, long-tail fields, conditional schemas |
| GLiNER-family zero-shot | none | tagger-scale | any flat entity schema, at volume |
| fine-tune an encoder | 2,000+ | tagger-scale | a stable schema you can afford to annotate |

: The zero-label options {tbl-colwidths="[28,14,18,40]"}

This chapter measured the first and the third. The middle row is the obvious
next measurement, and the one to run before you accept the 1,200× latency
penalty as the price of having no labels.

## Where BIO stops working {#sec-sequence-labeling-nested}

BIO assigns one label per token. That single sentence contains the format's
whole set of limitations, and real schemas hit all of them.

**Nested entities.** *Türkiye Cumhuriyeti Merkez Bankası* is an `ORG`, and
*Türkiye* inside it is a `LOC`. One token, two correct labels, and BIO has
room for one. Practically everyone drops the inner one and never mentions it;
biomedical and legal schemas, where nesting is the norm rather than the
exception, cannot.

**Overlapping entities.** Two spans that share tokens without one containing
the other — common in relation-heavy schemas and in clinical text.

**Discontinuous entities.** *sol ve sağ ventrikül* mentions two structures,
each of which is a span with a hole in it. Ordinary in clinical notes,
inexpressible in BIO.

The alternatives all give up the one-label-per-token constraint:

| approach | idea | cost |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Span enumeration | score every candidate span up to length *k*, classify each | $O(nk)$ candidates, which is $O(n^2)$ only when *k* grows with *n*; a strong, simple baseline |
| Biaffine / dependency-style | score every (start, end) pair with a biaffine layer [@yu2020named] | handles nesting natively; the standard strong result |
| MRC framing | ask "where are the organisations?" as a question per type [@li2020unified] | one forward pass per type; brings the type description into the model |
| Word-word grid tagging | classify the relation between every token pair — next-neighbour, tail-head [@li2022w2ner] | handles nesting and discontinuity in one formulation |
| Table filling / generative | emit the records directly as text | no span algebra at all — and back to the alignment problem above |

: Beyond one-label-per-token {tbl-colwidths="[26,42,32]"}

GLiNER-family models (@sec-sequence-labeling-llm) also return overlapping spans
natively, which makes the zero-shot route the cheapest way to find out whether
your schema needs a nesting-aware trainer at all.

How much you stand to lose is measurable before you decide: in the corpora
where nesting is annotated at all — GENIA, ACE — somewhere between a sixth and a
third of mentions are nested, so dropping the inner one is not a rounding error.
[If your schema has nesting and your pipeline uses BIO, you have already
decided to lose those entities.]{.hl} The decision is usually accidental,
inherited from a tutorial. Make it deliberately.

## Relations and events {#sec-sequence-labeling-relations}

Extracting *Ali* and *Acme* is half a record. The other half is that Ali
*works at* Acme.

The standard framing is pairwise classification: take every pair of mentions
in a sentence, and classify the relation between them, including a `no
relation` class that dominates the label distribution. It works, and it costs
$O(n^2)$ forward passes per sentence — the same quadratic that
@sec-sequence-labeling-nested has, for the same reason.

The three things worth knowing before starting:

1. **`no relation` is the overwhelming majority class**, so everything
   @sec-classification-imbalance said applies here with more force. Report
   micro-F1 *excluding* `no relation`, and expect the raw accuracy to be
   uninformative.
2. **Annotation cost dominates everything else.** Entity annotation is
   roughly linear in tokens; relation annotation is quadratic in entities,
   and the guidelines are far harder to make reproducible — two annotators
   who agree on `PER` and `ORG` routinely disagree on whether a sentence
   asserts employment. TACRED [@zhang2017position] is the reference dataset and
   the reference cautionary tale: re-annotating its development and test sets
   moved reported F1 by roughly eight points [@alt2020tacred], which measures the
   annotation noise rather than any model.
3. **Two limits worth stating out loud.** The pairwise framing above is
   *sentence-level*, and a large share of the relations in real documents cross
   sentence boundaries — that is the document-level setting, and it is
   meaningfully harder. And the framing assumes the mentions are already found,
   so every entity error upstream becomes a relation error downstream.

Event extraction adds a trigger word and a set of typed arguments, which is
the same machinery with more roles and worse agreement. For most applied work
in 2026 the honest advice is to try schema-guided generation first
(@sec-sequence-labeling-llm), measure it, and only build the pairwise
classifier if you can afford the annotation to beat it.

## Linking and normalization {#sec-sequence-labeling-linking}

Finding *Türkiye'nin* is recognition. Knowing that it refers to the same
thing as *Türkiye'de*, *Türkiye'deki* and *Türkiye* is
[entity linking](#gloss-entity-linking){#term-entity-linking .term-ref}, and
in an agglutinative language it starts one step earlier than the textbooks
assume.

::: {#gloss-entity-linking .column-margin .term-gloss}
**entity linking** — mapping a mention to a canonical identifier, so that
different surface forms of the same thing collapse to one record. Separate
from recognising that the mention is an entity at all.
[↩](#term-entity-linking){.term-back}
:::

Measured on this corpus's training half:

```text
entity mentions                             26,482
  carrying an apostrophe suffix              4,099   15.5%

distinct surface forms                      16,591
distinct after stripping the suffix         14,876   10.3% collapse

most common suffixes on mentions
  -da   587    -nın  352    -de   328    -ın   233
  -in   227    -a    201    -nin  195    -ya   182
```

[One mention in six carries a case suffix welded onto the name.]{.hl} And the
surface forms multiply per entity:

```text
base forms appearing in more than one surface form   1,122

  ABD       -> ABD, ABD'de, ABD'deki, ABD'li, ABD'nin, ...        13 forms
  Fransa    -> Fransa, Fransa'da, Fransa'daki, Fransa'dan, ...    12 forms
  Türkiye   -> Türkiye, Türkiye'de, Türkiye'deki, ...             12 forms
```

Count mentions of `ABD` by exact string and you get thirteen entities with
one occurrence each instead of one entity with thirteen. Every aggregate you
build on top — a frequency ranking, a co-occurrence graph, an alert on
"mentions of X this week" — is wrong in a way that looks plausible.

The Turkish-specific first step is cheap and worth doing before anything
clever: **split on the apostrophe and keep the stem.** It is not a general
solution — plenty of inflected mentions carry no apostrophe, and the
apostrophe convention is not universally followed — but it collapses 10.3% of
surface forms for one line of code.

Beyond that, the pipeline is the standard one: generate candidate entries
from a knowledge base by string similarity, then rank the candidates with
context. Classical systems did this with a graph over co-occurring mentions
[@hoffart2011robust]; the modern version encodes mention-in-context and
entry-description into the same vector space and retrieves
[@wu2020scalable] — which is @sec-embeddings' machinery, pointed at a
different problem. @sec-retrieval builds that retrieval step properly.

::: {.column-margin}
The evaluation trap here mirrors @sec-sequence-labeling-audit's. Linking
accuracy measured on mentions whose surface form appears in your knowledge
base is not linking accuracy; it is dictionary coverage. Report the two
separately, and report how often the correct entry was not a candidate at
all — that number is a ceiling nothing downstream can raise.
:::

## Intuition checks {#sec-sequence-labeling-intuition}

Answer these before reading the answers.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your tagger reports 96% token accuracy. Is it good?

You cannot tell, and the number is designed to stop you asking. On this
corpus a model that outputs `O` for every token scores **61.36%**, so 96%
represents 35 points of headroom, not 96 points of competence. On a realistic
corpus where most sentences contain no entity at all, the floor is higher
still — 97% or more is routine — and a model can beat it while finding
nothing.

Ask for span-level F1. If the answer is "we don't have that number", the
model has not been evaluated.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Token-level F1 is 88.73 and span-level F1 is 85.45. Where did three points go?

Boundaries. Token-level F1 gives partial credit: three correct tokens out of
a four-token organisation score three quarters. Span-level requires the type,
the first token and the last token all to match, so that same prediction
scores zero.

Do not read the gap as a boundary-error *rate*, though. It mixes several
things: partial overlaps, spans of different lengths counted token by token,
and type errors on long entities, all micro-averaged so that a four-token
mistake weighs four times a one-token one. It is a signal that boundary errors
are present, not a measurement of how many. If you want the number, count the
error types directly — exact, boundary-only, type-only, spurious, missed —
which is a twenty-line script and a far more actionable table. Report
span-level either way, because no downstream consumer can use three quarters of
a company name.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your transformer emits `O I-ORG I-ORG`. Whose bug is it?

Nobody's — it is the expected behaviour of a softmax tagger, which picks the
best label at each position independently with nothing coupling position 4 to
position 5. The best fine-tuned BERTurk in this chapter emits 139 such
transitions across 10,000 sentences, and a half-trained one emits 3,739.

What *is* your decision is what happens next. `seqeval` will silently recover
an `ORG` span; a strict decoder will drop it; a repair pass will rewrite the
first `I-` to `B-`. All three are defensible and they give different F1. The
bug is not the illegal transition, it is not knowing which of the three your
evaluation is doing.

Worth knowing how the count moves: it peaks at 3,739 when the model is
half-trained, falls to 139 at the full budget, and never reaches zero.
Well-formedness is something a softmax tagger learns approximately from data — a CRF scores whole sequences, so it rarely breaks the scheme, but a finite transition penalty is not a guarantee; a transition mask at decode time is.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. You have 200 labelled sentences. Fine-tune BERTurk or write a gazetteer?

Measured, on this corpus: fine-tuning 200 sentences gives **3.14 span F1**. A
dictionary of memorised strings gives **55.26**.

At that budget the encoder has seen a few hundred entities across six entity
tags plus `O`, with a randomly initialised head, and what it learns is to say `O` —
its token accuracy of 63.43% is barely above the 61.36% floor. The crossover
against a CRF trained on the full 20,000 sentences arrives somewhere between
**2,000 and 5,000** labelled sentences: at 2,000 the encoder is still a point
behind (84.23 against 85.45) and by 5,000 it is nearly three ahead.

So: gazetteer first, then a CRF, and fine-tune once you are past a few thousand
labelled sentences. The general lesson is that "just fine-tune a transformer"
is advice with a budget attached, and the budget is rarely stated.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Your NER F1 jumped six points when you switched corpora. Did the model improve?

Check for leakage before you celebrate. In WikiANN Turkish, **13.06% of test
sentences appear verbatim in the training set**, 1,305 of them with identical
gold labels. A memorising model gets those free.

The diagnostic takes four lines: hash your test inputs, intersect with your
training inputs, and score the leaked and clean halves separately. In this
chapter the CRF scored 99.81 on the leaked half against 83.56 on the clean
half. If your gap looks like that, you measured your dataset, not your model.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your LLM extractor returns a company that is not in the document. What is the F1 contribution?

It counts as a **false positive**, and the important part is that it must
count as something. Span metrics are defined over token offsets, and a string
with no offsets has nothing to compare against a gold span — which makes it
tempting to drop the row from the evaluation entirely. Do not: silently
discarding unalignable output prices invention at zero and flatters the
extractor. Either score it as a false positive against precision, or report an
explicit invalid-output rate alongside F1. Say in the protocol which you did.

But before you write "hallucination" in the report, check whose bug it is.
Measured here: of 1,419 returned mentions, 31 would not align — and 27 of
those were the *aligner's* fault, 20 from wiki markup in the corpus and 7
from a curly apostrophe normalised to a straight one. Only 4 in 1,419
(0.28%) were genuinely not in the text, and even those were case-suffix
confusions rather than invention.

So: count them, report the count, and split it by cause. It is a failure mode
a tagger structurally cannot have — a tagger can only label tokens that
exist — but most of what looks like it is preprocessing.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-sequence-labeling-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** Pages claiming to
list "the NER questions Google asks" are search-engine content with nothing
behind the claim. What follows are questions that recur in the two credible
open sources this book uses throughout — Chip Huyen's
[*Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews*](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/)
[@huyen2021interviews] and the
[Machine Learning Interviews](https://github.com/alirezadir/Machine-Learning-Interviews)
repository — plus the ones this chapter's own measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the task

**Q: Why is NER not just token classification?**

Because the output is spans and the model produces labels, so there is a
decoding step between them — and the decoding step is where the ambiguity
lives. Say what BIO buys (adjacent same-type entities become separable), what
it cannot express (nesting, overlap, discontinuity), and what a decoder does
with a malformed sequence. A candidate who says "it's just classification per
token" has not shipped one.

**Q: What is the CRF layer for, and do you still need it on top of BERT?**

The CRF models dependencies *between labels* — it learns a transition score
for every label pair and decodes with Viterbi, so it returns the best whole
sequence rather than the best label at each position. That makes an illegal
transition like `O → I-ORG` very expensive rather than merely unlikely — say
*expensive*, not *impossible*, because the transition scores are finite.

On top of a strong pre-trained encoder the gain is small, because the encoder
already sees the whole sentence and the transitions are mostly learnable from
context. Reported differences on top of strong encoders are typically under a
point on CoNLL-style benchmarks, but measure it on your own schema rather than
take that on trust — we did not measure it here. And say what the cheaper
option is: a transition mask over the logits plus Viterbi (@sec-sequence-labeling-bio)
rules out the illegal transitions at decode time
with no extra parameters and no retraining — and note that a guarantee needs
those transitions removed from the search space rather than merely penalised.

**Q: How would you evaluate an NER system?**

Span-level micro and macro F1, exact match, reported per type. Then say what
you would check *before* believing it: the everything-is-`O` floor, the
overlap between test and training inputs, and which decoding convention the
score assumes. Anyone who answers "F1" and stops has evaluated nothing.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Your NER model does well offline and badly in production. Walk through it.**

Ordered by cost, and the first three are not the model:

1. **Tokenization mismatch.** Offline you evaluated on pre-tokenized gold
   tokens; production tokenizes raw text with a different splitter, so the
   spans do not line up. This is the most common cause and the easiest to
   miss.
2. **Alignment.** Labels are per word, model inputs are per subword. Print
   one production sentence beside its aligned labels and read it.
3. **Domain.** Wikipedia fragments are not support tickets. 65.5% of the
   sentences this chapter trained on do not even end in punctuation.
4. **Leakage in the offline number.** See above; it inflates the memorising
   parts of your model most.
5. Only then, the model.

**Q: You need to extract 30 fields from contracts and have no labelled data.**

Start with schema-guided generation, because the alternative is months of
annotation before you learn whether the task is feasible. Then say how you
would know it works: hand-label a couple of hundred documents as an
evaluation set (evaluation data is far cheaper than training data), align
every returned string back onto the source, and count the ones that will not
align. Move to a trained extractor for the fields that are high-volume and
stable; keep generation for the long tail.

The answer to listen for is the evaluation set. Candidates who describe the
prompt and stop have not run one of these in production.

**Q: How do you handle an entity type that appears twice in your training data?**

You do not train it. Write a gazetteer or a rule, ship that, and collect
examples until there is something to train on. The measurement in this
chapter — 3.14 F1 at 200 sentences — is the general shape of the answer:
below a certain budget, learned models are worse than lists, and knowing
where that line is for your task is the actual skill.

match type *descriptions* against spans, so you get zero-shot extraction over an

1,200× number in it.

## Lab: extraction on a budget you actually have {#sec-sequence-labeling-lab}

The premise of this lab is the measurement in @sec-sequence-labeling-encoder:
at small label budgets the learned model loses to the list. The lab is
therefore not "fine-tune a transformer" — it is "find out what your budget
buys, before spending it".

Pick a domain where you can produce labelled sentences yourself: support
tickets, job ads, match reports, a bibliography. Choose three to five entity
types that a second person could label the same way.

### Step 1 — write the guidelines before labelling anything

One page. For each type: a definition, three positive examples, and three
near-misses that are *not* that type. @sec-data-annotation's argument in one
sentence: if the rule is not written down, the labels are not reproducible,
and the model is learning your Tuesday afternoon.

### Step 2 — label 300 sentences, and set aside 150 of them as test

Not 30. The evaluation set is the part you cannot skip, and it is worth more
than the training half at this budget — you can improve a model without more
training data, but you cannot measure one without evaluation data.

Label the test half *last*, and do not look at it again until step 6.

### Step 3 — compute the floor and the gazetteer

Everything-`O`, then longest-match over the strings in your training half.
Two numbers, half an hour, and they are the two numbers every later result
has to beat. Expect the gazetteer to be embarrassingly competitive.

### Step 4 — train a CRF, and check whether the features are doing anything

Use the feature template from @sec-sequence-labeling-baselines. Then ablate:
drop the suffix features, drop the context window, drop the shape feature,
and record the F1 each time. The point is not the final score; it is knowing
which part of your model is load-bearing.

### Step 5 — fine-tune an encoder at three budgets

50, 100 and 150 sentences from your training half. Plot span F1 against
budget. You are reproducing @sec-sequence-labeling-encoder's curve on your
own data, and the thing to look for is where — or whether — it crosses the
CRF.

### Step 6 — the schema-guided extractor, honestly

Put your guidelines in the prompt, constrain the output to a schema, and
verify the constraint is really applied by sending one request whose schema
the model would otherwise violate. Align every returned string back onto the
source. Report three numbers: span F1, the fraction of returned mentions that
would not align, and seconds per document.

### Step 7 — open the test set once

Score all five systems on the 150 held-out sentences. One table, one reading.

### What to hand in

The table, plus a paragraph naming which system you would ship and what it
would cost per thousand documents. If the gazetteer wins, say so — that is a
result, and on 150 labelled sentences it is a likely one.

## Exercises {#sec-sequence-labeling-exercises}

1. **Hand-decode a broken sequence.** Take the tags
   `O B-PER I-PER I-LOC O I-ORG B-ORG` over a seven-token sentence. Write out
   the spans a lenient decoder produces, then a strict one. Which tokens do
   the two disagree about, and how many spans does each return?

2. **Token versus span F1.** Take one system's predictions and compute both.
   Explain the gap in terms of boundary errors, and construct a prediction
   that scores well on the first and zero on the second.

3. **Break the alignment on purpose.** Take the alignment code from
   @sec-sequence-labeling-alignment and remove the `word_ids()` call, zipping
   labels to subwords positionally instead. Train on 2,000 sentences both
   ways and report both scores. Then find the shortest sentence in your data
   where the two labelings differ, and print it.

4. **Measure the leakage yourself.** Hash the token sequences of any NER
   corpus you use — CoNLL-2003 [@tjongkimsang2003conll], your own, or
   WikiANN in another language — and report the test/train intersection. Then
   score a memorising baseline separately on the leaked and clean halves.

5. **The suffix ablation.** Remove `w[-3:]`, `w[-2:]` and `w.hasapos` from
   the CRF features and re-fit. How much of the 85.45 was Turkish
   orthography? Predict the answer before you run it.

6. **Normalize the mentions.** Take the extracted mentions from any system,
   collapse them on the apostrophe, and count how many distinct entities you
   have before and after. Then find a mention the heuristic gets *wrong* —
   they exist, and describing one is the exercise.

7. **Nesting, on paper.** Write five sentences from your own domain that
   contain a nested entity. Encode them in BIO, then in a span-enumeration
   format, and state precisely what BIO lost.

Before anything else: check your benchmark for train/test overlap. It takes
twenty lines, it is the first thing this chapter did, and it changed how every
later number should be read.

## What to remember {#sec-sequence-labeling-summary}

- **Compute the floor.** Everything-is-`O` scores **61.36% token accuracy**
  and **0.00 span F1** on this corpus, and higher on a realistic one where
  most sentences contain no entity. Every token-accuracy number in sequence
  labelling should be read as a distance from that floor, and the distance is
  usually smaller than the headline suggests.

- **Report span-level F1.** Token accuracy 94.41, token-level F1 88.73,
  span-level F1 85.45 — the same predictions, three answers. Only the last
  one asks whether the record came out right.

- **Audit the corpus before you trust the score.** WikiANN Turkish has
  **13.06% of its test set verbatim in training**, and the leakage bonus
  falls monotonically with how much a system memorises: **+26.50** for a
  gazetteer, **+16.25** for the CRF (99.81 leaked against 83.56 clean),
  **+7.65** for the fine-tuned encoder. That gap is a measurement of how much
  of a score is recall of the training set. Hash your test inputs — it is
  four lines.

- **The classical baseline is not a formality.** A gazetteer scores **55.26**
  from a Python dictionary; a CRF with hand features scores **85.45** in
  **18.5 seconds on a CPU**. Fine-tuned BERTurk needs 2,000 to 5,000 labelled
  sentences to match the CRF trained on 20,000, and reaches **91.92** on the
  full budget — a real saving, and a real threshold below which the
  transformer is simply the worse model.

- **200 labelled sentences buys single-digit span F1** — 3.14 in our single
  run, and the seed-to-seed spread at that budget is wide, so read the order of
  magnitude rather than the decimals. Not 60, not 40. At that budget a
  fine-tuned encoder learns to say `O`, and a memorised list beats it by fifty
  points. "Just fine-tune a transformer" is advice with a budget
  attached; ask what the budget is.

- **Decoding is a decision you are making whether or not you know it.** A
  softmax tagger at full budget emitted **139 illegal BIO transitions**
  across 10,000 sentences — and 3,739 when half-trained; the CRF emitted zero at every budget, because Viterbi scores whole sequences and a forbidden transition with no supporting features does not make the winning path — an empirical zero, not a guarantee; mask the transitions if you need one. What your evaluation does with those 139 changes your
  reported F1, and the convention is not stated in most papers.

- **Alignment is where the silent bugs live.** Entity words fragment into
  **1.98 subwords each in BERTurk against 1.45 for ordinary words** — names
  are rare, so tokenizers break them. Get `word_ids()` wrong and the model
  still trains, the loss still falls, and the labels are attached to the
  wrong tokens.

- **A schema guarantees shape, never truth.** `ollama` 0.24.0 silently
  ignored a JSON schema on `/api/chat` while enforcing it on `/api/generate`,
  and the enforced call happily returned `{"answer": 1}` for the capital of
  France. Send one request the model would otherwise fail, and check.

- **Zero-shot extraction is where you start, not where you stop.** On the
  same 1,000 sentences: LLM **60.57** span F1 with no labels at all,
  gazetteer 54.90, CRF **84.16**, fine-tuned encoder **91.44** — and the LLM
  is about **1,200× slower per sentence**. It beats the dictionary and loses
  to eighteen seconds of CRF by 24 points. Its worst class is `ORG` recall at
  40.10, because a prompt cannot encode the boundary convention that 20,000
  annotated examples teach.

- **An LLM returns strings; a metric wants offsets.** Every mention has to be
  aligned back onto the source, and that step is where you can quietly
  misattribute your own bugs: 27 of 31 alignment failures here were the
  aligner's, not the model's. Fixing it moved F1 by 0.28 — so check it, and
  do not expect it to explain a bad number.
